series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 1/1] mm/swap: allocate contiguous swap slots for a reclaim batch
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes swap slot allocation by allocating contiguous slots in batches, reducing the number of small write requests and improving performance. It achieves this by recording the number of pages of each order that need a slot before swapping out a batch, and then making those allocations follow contiguous free slots. This approach helps to minimize the fragmentation of swap clusters and reduces the overhead of small write requests.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concerns that the patch does not address workloads that benefit more from disk swapping than compression swapping, and requested further consideration for these use cases.

Reviewer noted that the patch does not apply its contiguous allocation heuristic to folios larger than a certain order, and found this omission reasonable.

Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concern that the patch's preference for non-full clusters with contiguous slots may lead to increased lock contention, especially as swapfiles become more fragmented.

Reviewer Nhat Pham raised concerns about the effectiveness of the contiguous swap slot allocation heuristic, questioning whether it would lead to overshooting the estimate and creating problems down the line. They also suggested that this heuristic might not be necessary for cgroups that enable zswap or zram.
review_comments.raw_body:
Thanks for looking into this! There are still workloads that benefit
more from disk swapping than compression swapping... We should make
the swap subsystem work for them.

I haven't read the code too closely, as it's an RFC meant to show the
general idea. So I'll just make some comments and ask some questions
about the idea:

---

Ah so we don't invoke this heuristics for folio larger than certain
orders? Makes sense.

---

So we prefer non-full clusters with contiguous slots, over free
clusters, over other nonfull clusters.

I think this part makes sense to me FWIW. We do skip fast path and go
for slow paths more often, so do make sure we're not paying with too
much lock contention, especially as the swapfile fils or get more
fragmented (which this patch series does nudge us towards). But FWIW,
we pretty much go back to the old behavior the moment we fail to find
contiguity for the first time in the batch, so I think we'll be
fine...?

---

Some general questions:

1. How many pages in folio_list typically do get reclaimed? There can
be quite a few with references, which we rotate/promote, when we scan,
right? Would constantly overshooting the estimate create problem down
the line?

(This is one of the few places where indirection (vswap) would have
helped - we can collect a batch of pages after unmapping, then pass
them to the phys swap allocator (after checking zswappability, etc.).
Maybe we can solve it better after it's landed, and accept an
imperfect solution for now?)

2. Should we skip this heuristics for cgroups that enables zswap (and
maybe zram)? Contiguity matters less there... unless it help at
writeback time? Hard to say without experimentation - maybe you can do
the same check you did for your zswap writeback batching patch series?

review_comments.author: Alexandre Ghiti
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that the folio_alloc_swap_split() function is not properly handling the case where a batch of LRU-adjacent folios spans multiple free clusters, and requested that the function be modified to allocate contiguous swap slots for such cases.

Reviewer Alexandre Ghiti noted that large folios have a separate allocation scheme and suggested adding this detail to the changelog.

Reviewer Alexandre Ghiti expressed a neutral sentiment by stating they would investigate the impact of this patch on zswap and writeback, but did not provide any specific technical concerns or suggestions.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch aims to reduce the number of I/O requests on a swap device by keeping reclaim batches contiguous. The current implementation of swap allocation and deallocation can lead to scattered writes, resulting in increased I/O requests. The patch modifies the allocator to allocate contiguous free slots for a reclaim batch, reducing the number of small requests and improving throughput. This is achieved by informing the allocator about the size of the batch and allowing it to allocate contiguous slots accordingly. The goal is to reduce the overhead of swap I/O operations and improve system performance.

review_comments.summary: Reviewer Kairui Song suggested reverting commit 9a42aed48421, which prefers nonfull over free clusters for small order allocations, and instead always scanning full clusters to prioritize contiguity on large physical swap devices.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Alexandre,

That's a interesting problem. I think the real problem is with commit
9a42aed48421 ("mm, swap: prefer nonfull over free clusters"), right?

It's more like a balance between fragmentation and contiguity of small
order allocation issue.

Perhaps we should instead always scan the full clusters and revert
that one commit? That commit was only following the idea of keeping
the allocation more compacted for that series, it looked good at that
time. Since fragmentation issues can be solved in other ways,
contiguity seems to matter more for large physical swap devices.

I encountered this myself. Remember when I wrote my own swap allocator
for vswap? In one of the version, I went for free clusters first
instead of partial clusters. It fragmented the swap space, so I had to
copy your homework and went for partially used clusters first...

Anyway, maybe I'm wrong - some numbers would be nice here.

review_comments.summary:
Reviewer suggested limiting the patch's scope to SYNC devices or exploring simpler solutions to address the problem, expressing skepticism about the significance of a 4% reduction in mTHP failures.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 01/12] mm/page_alloc: reset can_retry_reserves when the slowpath restarts
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the page allocation mechanism in the Linux kernel by resetting a flag called can_retry_reserves when the slowpath restarts after certain events, such as cpuset updates or zonelist rebuilds. The goal is to ensure that memory allocations are retried correctly even in the presence of these events.

review_comments.author: Zi Yan
review_comments.summary: Approved the patch with a positive sentiment, indicating that it is ready for merge.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Sat Oct 31, 2026 at 10:13 PM EDT, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> Commit 2c4c3e29897d ("mm/page_alloc: simplify __alloc_pages_slowpath()
> flow") retries an allocation once with reserve_flags when the caller
> becomes eligible for reserves, guarded by can_retry_reserves.
>
> A restart after a cpuset update or a zonelist rebuild retries with
> can_retry_reserves already set to false, so a caller that cannot
> reclaim (GFP_NOWAIT | __GFP_MEMALLOC), fails without trying reserves.
>
> Reset can_retry_reserves on restart. Only a cpuset or zonelist change
> restarts the slowpath, so the retry still runs at most once per change.
>
> With a kprobe helping to make the race deterministic, an allocation
> can be made to return NULL. With this patch the allocation will succeed.
>
> Fixes: 2c4c3e29897d ("mm/page_alloc: simplify __alloc_pages_slowpath() flow")

series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents the pagesets of an empty zone from being freed prematurely, which can cause corruption when a new owner takes over the per-cpu memory. Instead, it keeps the existing pagesets and allows setup_zone_pageset() to reuse them. This fix addresses a problem introduced by a previous commit that freed the pagesets when a zone became empty.

series_items.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the accuracy of oom detection tracepoints by passing the zone pointer instead of the zoneref pointer in the reclaim_retry_zone tracepoint. This change is necessary because memory hotplug rebuilds the zonelists in place while allocations are under way, which can lead to incorrect zone identification.

review_comments.summary: Identified the problem with zonelist rebuilds and agreed that passing the zone pointer is a good solution.

> to the reclaim_retry_zone tracepoint, which loads the zone from the

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 04/12] mm/page_alloc: detect zonelist rebuilds from memory hot-add
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a memory hot-add issue in the Linux kernel's page allocation mechanism. Specifically, it detects zonelist rebuilds from memory hot-add and fixes a race condition between build_all_zonelists and page allocation. The fix involves gating sequence checks on CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG to cover all configurations that rebuild zonelists after boot.

review_comments.author: Zi Yan
review_comments.summary: Acknowledged the patch with Acked-by, indicating they are satisfied with its technical quality and content.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Sat Oct 31, 2026 at 10:13 PM EDT, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> The zonelist_update_seq retry was limited to CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE,
> presumably because only hot-remove takes zones out of a zonelist.
>
> However, build_zonerefs_node() rewrites the zonelists in place, so
> onlining the first block of a zone shifts the entries that follow it
> in every zonelist containing that zone.  This can cause a spurious
> allocation failure for a __GFP_THISNODE caller.
>
> For a node with only ZONE_NORMAL, onlining its first ZONE_MOVABLE block
> rewrites the node's ZONELIST_NOFALLBACK list as:
>
>   [NORMAL, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NORMAL, NULL]
>
> A concurrent GFP_KERNEL | __GFP_THISNODE allocation can observe the
> intermediate list, skip ZONE_MOVABLE, and find no eligible zone. With
> CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE=n, check_retry_zonelist() returns 0 and the
> allocation fails even though the node has free ZONE_NORMAL memory.
>
> Gate the sequence checks on CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG, which covers every
> configuration that rebuilds zonelists after boot.
>
> Fixes: 3d36424b3b58 ("mm/page_alloc: fix race condition between build_all_zonelists and page allocation")
> Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
> Reviewed-by: Vlastimil Babka (SUSE) <vbabka@kernel.org>

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 05/12] mm/mmzone: read the zoneref slot once in zonelist_zone()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a memory hotplug issue where zonelists are rebuilt in place, causing the zoneref slot to change between loads. It uses READ_ONCE() to ensure that the zone is loaded only once.

review_comments.author: Zi Yan
review_comments.summary: Identified the issue and approved the fix, suggesting that READ_ONCE() is sufficient to prevent the zoneref slot from changing between loads.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Sat Oct 31, 2026 at 10:13 PM EDT, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> Memory hotplug rebuilds zonelists in place while allocations walk them,
> so a zoneref slot can change between two loads of it.
>
> zonelist_zone() loads the slot with a plain access.  The compiler may
> load it again later instead of keeping the zone it already read, so a
> caller can check one zone and then use another, or the NULL terminator.
>
> Use READ_ONCE().  Callers that take a zone from a slot and keep using
> it, such as get_page_from_freelist() with ac->preferred_zoneref, need
> that single load.
>
> Fixes: 11cd8638c37f ("mm, page_alloc: remove stop_machine from build_all_zonelists")

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 06/12] mm/page_alloc: snapshot the preferred zone against shrink rebuilds
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a kernel NULL pointer dereference bug in the page allocation code by introducing a snapshot of the preferred zone against concurrent zonelist rebuilds. The preferred zone is read only once, and if it becomes stale or NULL due to concurrent rebuilds, the function fails as expected. This fix removes the need for repeated reads of the preferred zone, which can lead to bugs like the one reported.

This change fixes an issue where kprobes holding the walk across the online could cause a fault to take a page from the wrong node.

The zonelist_update_seq retry was limited to CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE,
presumably because only hot-remove takes zones out of a zonelist.

However, build_zonerefs_node() rewrites the zonelists in place, so
onlining the first block of a zone shifts the entries that follow it
in every zonelist containing that zone.  This can cause a spurious
allocation failure for a __GFP_THISNODE caller.

For a node with only ZONE_NORMAL, onlining its first ZONE_MOVABLE block
rewrites the node's ZONELIST_NOFALLBACK list as:

  [NORMAL, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NORMAL, NULL]

intermediate list, skip ZONE_MOVABLE, and find no eligible zone. With
CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE=n, check_retry_zonelist() returns 0 and the
allocation fails even though the node has free ZONE_NORMAL memory.

configuration that rebuilds zonelists after boot.

zone->per_cpu_pageset and zone->per_cpu_zonestats. Nothing waits for those
who found the zone populated and still use the two pointers. They take
neither the memory hotplug lock nor any other lock which offline_pages()
holds, and some of them can sleep:

    for_each_populated_zone(zone)

      cond_resched()
                                      adjust_present_page_count()
                                      zone_pcp_reset(zone)
                                        free_percpu(zone->per_cpu_pageset)
      decay_pcp_high(zone, pcp)
      __this_cpu_write(pcp->expire, 0)

zone_pcp_update(), show_free_areas() and the readers and writers of the
zonestats. If the per-cpu memory has got a new owner in the meantime, it
is corrupted.

leak them when the zone gets memory again. Keep them instead and let
setup_zone_pageset() and zone_pcp_init() use them again, like it is done

have been calculated for a zone without memory by the
init_per_zone_wmark_min() of offline_pages(), which is what
setup_zone_pageset() would come up with as well.

Memory hotplug rebuilds zonelists in place while allocations walk them,
so a zoneref slot can change between two loads of it.

zonelist_zone() loads the slot with a plain access.  The compiler may
load it again later instead of keeping the zone it already read, so a
caller can check one zone and then use another, or the NULL terminator.

Use READ_ONCE().  Callers that take a zone from a slot and keep using
it, such as get_page_from_freelist() with ac->preferred_zoneref, need
that single load.

@@ -1855,7 +1855,8 @@ extern struct zone *next_zone(struct zone *zone);

 {
-	return zoneref->zone;
+	/* Memory hotplug rewrites zonelists in place. */
+	return READ_ONCE(zoneref->zone);
 }

__next_zones_zonelist() tests a slot's zone for NULL, then reads the
slot again to look up the zone's node. Offlining a zone's last block
rebuilds the zonelists in place, so the second read can return the
terminator:

  CPU 0                             CPU 1
  __next_zones_zonelist(nodemask)
    zonelist_zone(slot 1) = NORMAL
                                    offline_pages()
                                      build_all_zonelists()
                                        [MOVABLE, NORMAL, NULL]
                                        -> [NORMAL, NULL]
    zref_in_nodemask(slot 1)
      zone_to_nid(NULL)

Current GCC and clang merge the two reads, but nothing requires it.
With mm/mmzone.o built with -fno-inline -fno-ipa-sra, holding a
nodemask allocation between the reads while the node's last movable
block goes offline oopses every time:

  RIP: 0010:zone_to_nid+0x0/0x10
  Call Trace:
   zref_in_nodemask+0x9/0x20
   __next_zones_zonelist+0x23/0x70
   prepare_alloc_pages.constprop.0+0x16c/0x190
   __alloc_frozen_pages_noprof+0xaf/0x330

Onlining the first block of a zone rebuilds every zonelist in place,
shifting the slots after the new zone.  The iterator approves a slot,
then the allocator loads the zone from it, so a GFP_KERNEL request can
land in ZONE_MOVABLE and a nodemask request on a node outside its mask:

  CPU 0                             CPU 1
  prepare_alloc_pages()
    first_zones_zonelist(nodemask {1})
      slot 0 (NORMAL1) approved
                                    online_pages()
                                      build_all_zonelists()
                                        [NORMAL1, NORMAL2, ...]
                                        -> [MOVABLE1, NORMAL1, ...]
  get_page_from_freelist()
    zone = zonelist_zone(slot 0)    /* MOVABLE1 */
    allocates from MOVABLE1

zonelist_update_seq detects the rebuild, but only the slowpath's failure
exits check it.

Check it whenever an allocation succeeds too, and if it changed, free
the page and retry, as the memcg charge failure path does.  Eligible
pages are dropped as well: zonelists only change when memory comes or
goes, and a retry is simpler than rechecking the page.

Freeing the page does not undo a block the allocation claimed.  A
GFP_KERNEL request that lands in a fresh ZONE_MOVABLE converts a free
block to MIGRATE_UNMOVABLE, which stays until the zone's movable free
list runs out and a movable allocation takes it back.

The fast and bulk paths read the seqlock's raw seqcount without waiting:
an ALLOC_NOLOCK caller can be an NMI that interrupted the writer, and on
PREEMPT_RT the seqlock accessor takes the spinlock.  A sample taken
mid-write costs a retry, or NULL under ALLOC_NOLOCK.
check_retry_zonelist() returns 0 when compiled out, so a backport
without the hot-add change stays harmless.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 1/4] mm/huge_memory: scale thp_underused() to the folio size
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the thp_underused() function to be aware of the size of a folio, rather than just PMD-sized folios. It scales the khugepaged_max_ptes_none threshold proportionally to the number of pages in the folio, ensuring that the same fraction of zero-filled pages is tolerated for any folio size. This change will prevent issues when collapsing mTHP orders and splitting folios, as both operations would use the same threshold for a given folio size. The patch makes no functional changes for PMD-sized folios, as their page count is always HPAGE_PMD_NR.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 2/4] mm/huge_memory: don't queue folios when underused splitting is inactive
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the handling of anonymous PMD-sized folios in huge memory by skipping their queueing when underused splitting is inactive, which is the default configuration. This change is motivated by the fact that at the default sysctl maximum, no folio is ever underused and thus there's no need to queue them for splitting. The patch also factors out this check into a new function `thp_underused_never()` to share it between two functions.

review_comments.author: Usama Arif
review_comments.summary: Acknowledged the patch as reasonable and noted that in production environments, the sysctl value is rarely changed during application runtime. Added an Acked-by tag.
review_comments.raw_body:
On 03/11/2026 21:20, Joanne Koong wrote:
> Every anonymous PMD-sized folio is put on the deferred split queue when
> it is first mapped, so that the shrinker can find it under memory
> pressure and split it if it turns out to be mostly zero-filled.
> 
> With the default khugepaged/max_ptes_none this is wasted work. The
> default is HPAGE_PMD_NR - 1, which tells thp_underused() that any number
> of zero-filled pages is tolerable, which means the shrinker will never
> split any of these folios for being underused. They take the list_lru
> lock at fault time, inflate the object count the shrinker reports, and
> are then walked and dropped when they're first scanned.
> 
> Skip the queueing when khugepaged/max_ptes_none is at its maximum, and
> factor that check out into thp_underused_never() so that
> deferred_split_folio() and thp_underused() share it. Since the default
> is the maximum, out of the box no folio is queued for underused
> splitting at all, PMD-sized ones included. Partially mapped folios are
> still queued as before.
> 
> This also matters for a subsequent patch that adds anonymous mTHP folios
> to the deferred split list, as it keeps systems running the default from
> paying for that on every anonymous fault.
> 
> Please note that the queue has always been best-effort. A folio that was
> queued before khugepaged/max_ptes_none is lowered gets dropped from the
> queue by the first scan that finds it's not underused, so changing the
> sysctl has never retroactively applied to folios that were already
> scanned. Requeueing eligible folios when the sysctl changes will be
> addressed in a separate patch.
> 
> Suggested-by: Johannes Weiner <hannes@cmpxchg.org>
> Suggested-by: David Hildenbrand <david@kernel.org>
> Signed-off-by: Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com>
> ---

This sounds reasonable. In production, as far as I know from speaking with folks
in conferences, no one changes the value during application runtime
(atleast this is true in meta). Its usually only changed before the workload
starts (or just at boot time).

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 3/4] mm/huge_memory: add a per-order counter for underused splits

The existing thp_underused_split_page counter only counts PMD-sized folios, but this change introduces a new split_underused stat that tracks underused splits of all sizes. This is done to match the behavior of other THP split stats and provide more accurate information about huge page usage. series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 4/4] mm: add anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series adds anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list, addressing memory regressions caused by underused splitting in systems with large THPs. The change mirrors existing behavior for PMD-sized folios and introduces a hardcoded minimum size of 2M for underused splitting.

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary: Expressed agreement that a hardcoded 2MB minimum size for underused splitting is a better starting point, and applied the Reviewed-by tag.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed, Nov 4, 2026 at 5:20 AM Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Unlike for PMD-sized folios, an anonymous mTHP folio doesn't get added
> to the deferred split list at fault or collapse time. As a result, a
> fully mapped mTHP folio that is mostly zero-filled doesn't get split by
> the deferred split shrinker when the system is under memory pressure.
>
> At Meta we would like to deploy 2M THP=always on arm64 with 64k base
> pages, as 2M gives the contpte benefits while the PMD size (512M) is too
> big to use. Without underused splitting this causes memory regressions,
> as the unused parts of those folios can never be broken down and
> reclaimed.
>
> Add anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list from
> map_anon_folio_pte_nopf(), mirroring what map_anon_folio_pmd_nopf()
> already does for PMD-sized folios. This covers both the fault path and
> the khugepaged mTHP collapse path. If there is memory pressure, a
> zero-filled mTHP can then be split with its zero pages remapped to the
> shared zero page and reclaimed.
>
> Only queue mTHP folios of at least 2M for underused splitting. With
> thp_underused() scaling khugepaged/max_ptes_none to the folio size, any
> folio of order 2 or above could in principle be underused, but for small
> folios it is unlikely to be worth it. An order-2 folio on 4k base pages
> can free at most four pages and on systems that only enable small mTHP
> sizes (eg Android's order-2-only configuration) zero-filled subpages
> tend to be few and short-lived.
>
> The minimum is hard-coded rather than a knob, since admins have no good
> way of choosing it, and is a size rather than an order since what a
> split recovers depends on the folio's size in bytes, and the same order
> means very different sizes across different base page sizes. It can be
> lowered later if data shows smaller sizes are worth it. PMD-sized folios
> are exempt from the minimum in order to maintain backwards compatibility
> since on some architectures (s390, with a 1M PMD) the PMD size can be
> below 2M.
>
> To minimize overhead on the common order-0 fault path, the
> deferred_split_folio() call is guarded by an inline folio_test_large()
> check.
>
> Suggested-by: Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev>
> Signed-off-by: Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com>
> ---

I believe we discussed this before and agreed that a
hardcoded 2MB would be a better starting point.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 2/7] mm/page_counter: introduce per-CPU stock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a per-CPU stock representation in the page_counter layer, similar to memcg's seven-slot per-CPU stock. It adds a new struct page_counter_stock_pcp that preserves the existing behavior from memcg and includes a backpointer to the base of the percpu stock. The patch also updates the page_counter structure to include pointers to the percpu stock and its owning cgroup_subsys_state. No functional changes are intended in this patch, which is part of a larger series.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 3/7] mm/page_counter: make page_counter_try_charge() stock-aware
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the page_counter_try_charge function to be aware of stock, allowing it to consume stock transparently while preserving existing semantics. Two new parameters are added: may_batch and nr_charged. The first parameter preserves the behavior in !allow_spinning scenarios, where charges are made as quickly as possible without evicting other stock slots. The second parameter reflects the size of a successful hierarchy charge, used for memory.high accounting heuristics.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 4/7] mm/memcontrol: check PF_MEMALLOC after trying the limits
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the behavior of memory charging in Linux to check for PF_MEMALLOC after trying limits, rather than before. This change is necessary because a later patch moves the memory stock into the page counter, leaving no room between consuming the stock and trying limits for the PF_MEMALLOC check. The patch checks for PF_MEMALLOC on both outcomes of the page counter charge, skipping memory.high on success and forcing the charge on failure.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 5/7] mm/memcontrol: move memory stock to page counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the memory stock from memcg to page counters, allowing for more efficient and accurate memory management. The change preserves the legacy user-visible relationship between memory and swap usage, even when their raw values temporarily diverge. It also introduces a new logic to prevent reclaiming swap space when both memory and swap have equal limits. The patch removes unused code from memcg and prepares it for future work on introducing additional page counters without breaking the fast path.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 6/7] mm/memcontrol: add stock to the memsw page counter
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a separate stock to the memsw page counter, allowing it to operate independently of the memory bank. The common drain scheduling is factored into schedule_stock_drain(), which handles both stocks uniformly. If memory charge fails, only the nr_pages from memsw are rolled back. This change enables the raw counters for memory and memsw to temporarily drift due to cached amounts, while preserving the user-visible cgroup-v1 invariant.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 7/7] mm/memcontrol: restrict memory stock to leaf cgroups on v2
series_items.patch_summary: This patch restricts memory stock to leaf cgroups in the new page_counter_stock world, ensuring that stock does not get stranded in the hierarchy and cannot be used by processes that actually charge. It achieves this by preventing stock from accumulating in non-leaf page_counters through three methods: clearing the parent's memory stock pointer, scheduling drains for non-isolated CPUs, and lazily cleaning up CPUs that are not drained due to isolation or racing with a refill. The patch also re-enables stock when a parent becomes a leaf again.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series moves the stock implementation from memcontrol to page_counter, allowing for better separation of charge caching and policy management. The stock is a per-CPU cache of precharged pages that speeds up small allocations by avoiding frequent walks of the page_counter hierarchy. By moving it to page_counter, the patch simplifies the handling of stock in non-leaf cgroups and prepares for future improvements. It also ensures that locking behavior remains unchanged and that exact charging is preserved for non-spinning callers.
